candidates.teaser: The moment you learn a new word, the entire world starts whispering it back at you — and science knows exactly why.
candidates.video_title: Why the Universe Repeats Words You Just Learned
candidates.video_description: The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon makes newly learned information appear everywhere right after you first notice it. It's not coincidence — it's your brain playing a silent trick on reality. Neuroscientists have mapped exactly how this cognitive glitch works.
candidates.script: You learn a new word at noon. By midnight, you've heard it five times. That is not a coincidence — your brain literally rewired itself to hunt it. It's called the Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon, and it kicks in the instant your brain flags something as new. Your reticular activating system starts filtering reality, pulling that word out of the noise that was always there. The world didn't change. Your brain quietly decided what you're allowed to notice. So — what has yours been hiding from you?

candidates.topic: The Death of the Last Titan — Paraceratherium
candidates.teaser: The largest land mammal that ever walked Earth vanished, and the reason is stranger than any extinction story you've heard.
candidates.video_title: The Biggest Land Animal Ever — Then It Just Vanished
candidates.video_description: Paraceratherium stood nearly five meters tall and weighed over 20 tons, dwarfing any elephant alive today. For millions of years it ruled Asia — until the ground itself betrayed it. Its extinction story rewrites what we thought we knew about climate and giants.
candidates.script: Twenty tons. Five meters tall. It made a modern elephant look like a deer. Paraceratherium was the largest land mammal that ever lived, and it dominated Asia for over 11 million years. Then, around 23 million years ago, the Tibetan Plateau started rising. It reshaped wind patterns, dried out grasslands, and swallowed the creature's entire world. The biggest animal on land wasn't killed by a predator or a meteor — it was erased by a mountain slowly growing. Could the same thing happen today?

candidates.topic: The Woman Who Remembered Everything — Hyperthymesia
candidates.teaser: She can tell you exactly what she ate for lunch on March 14th, 1988 — and she cannot forget a single day of her life, even if she tries.
candidates.video_title: She Cannot Forget a Single Day of Her Entire Life
candidates.video_description: Jill Price was the first person ever diagnosed with hyperthymesia — a condition where the brain records every single day in perfect, involuntary detail. She described it not as a gift, but as a burden. Scientists studying her brain found something deeply unexpected.
candidates.script: She remembers every single day of her life since age fourteen — not vaguely, perfectly. Ask Jill Price what happened on October 29th, 1983, and she'll tell you the weather, the news, what she felt. Scientists called it hyperthymesia, the first confirmed case ever recorded. When they scanned her brain, the regions tied to memory were physically enlarged. She didn't see it as a superpower. She called it exhausting — like a movie she can never turn off. Would you want a memory like that?

candidates.topic: The Ocean With No Salt — Lake Baikal Depths
candidates.teaser: At the bottom of the world's deepest lake lives a creature that should be impossible — and it has never once needed the ocean.
candidates.video_title: The Deep-Sea Animal Trapped Inside a Lake
candidates.video_description: Lake Baikal holds 20% of all unfrozen freshwater on Earth and plunges 1,642 meters deep — deeper than most ocean trenches people visit. At its floor lives the Baikal seal, the only freshwater seal on the planet, 1,600 kilometers from any sea. How it got there has baffled scientists for over a century.
candidates.script: At the bottom of a Siberian lake, 1,642 meters down, lives a seal — the only freshwater seal on Earth. Lake Baikal is deeper than most ocean trenches, holds a fifth of all liquid freshwater on the planet, and is 1,600 kilometers from the nearest sea. Scientists still debate how the Baikal seal got there. The leading theory: an ancient river corridor that vanished millions of years ago, trapping its ancestors inside. It has been sealed in ever since. Nature built a ocean in the middle of a continent — and filled it with monsters.

candidates.topic: The Color Blind Artist Who Chose to Stay Blind — Neil Harbisson
candidates.teaser: A doctor implanted an antenna into his skull to let him hear colors — and when they offered to cure him, he said no.
candidates.video_title: He Hears Colors Through a Chip in His Skull
candidates.video_description: Neil Harbisson was born completely colorblind, seeing only in grayscale. A surgeon implanted an antenna into his occipital bone that converts light frequencies into sound vibrations directly in his skull. He became the first person officially recognized as a cyborg by a government — and when a cure was offered, he refused it.
candidates.script: He was born seeing only in grey. So a surgeon drilled an antenna into his skull, fusing it directly to the bone. It converts color frequencies into sound vibrations he feels through his jaw. Neil Harbisson became the first government-recognized cyborg on Earth — his antenna is on his passport photo. He can hear ultraviolet. He can hear infrared. Colors humans will never see. When doctors offered him a cure, he refused. He said he no longer wanted to see color. He wanted to hear it. Is that still a disability?
